summary.text: A probability mass function gives the probability that a discrete random variable is exactly equal to some value.
It is often the main way of defining a discrete probability distribution, for single variables or several at once.
Thinking of probability as mass helps avoid mistakes, since the total probability over all outcomes is conserved just as physical mass is.

facts.label: What it gives
facts.value: Probability that a variable equals a value exactly

facts.label: Mode
facts.value: The value with the largest probability mass

facts.label: Binomial example
facts.value: Chance of exactly one 6 in three die rolls

facts.label: Geometric example
facts.value: Tossing a coin until the first heads appears

facts.label: Where it is zero
facts.value: Zero for all but a countable number of values

items.prompt: A variable records the number shown on a die roll. What does its mass function tell you when you put in the number 4?

options.label: The chance that the roll is 4 or lower
The chance that the roll is exactly 4
The average of all the possible rolls
How likely a roll is to land near 4 per unit length

items.explain: A probability mass function gives the probability that a discrete variable is exactly equal to the value you put in.

items.prompt: In a quiz, the mass function for scores is largest at a score of 7. What is 7 called?
items.explain: The value of the random variable with the largest probability mass is called the mode.

items.prompt: You flip a coin over and over until the first heads shows up, and record how many flips it took. Which distribution models that number?
items.explain: The geometric distribution describes the number of trials needed to get one success, such as tossing a coin until the first heads.

items.prompt: You pull one marble from a bag of red, green and blue marbles and record its colour. Which distribution models a single draw like this?
items.explain: When a discrete distribution has two or more categories, one of which may occur in a single trial (draw), it is a categorical distribution.

items.prompt: You roll a fair die three times and count how many sixes appear. Which distribution models that count of successes?
items.explain: The binomial distribution models the number of successes in n independent draws that each have two possible outcomes, such as getting exactly one 6 in three rolls.

items.prompt: A smooth measurement, such as a scale reading that can be any value in a range, is a continuous variable. What is the chance it equals exactly one given value?

options.label: Equal to the mass function at that value
It depends on how common the value is

items.explain: For a continuous random variable the probability of any single exact value is zero. That is why a mass function is used only for discrete variables.

paragraphs.heading: Probability at a point
paragraphs.text: A probability mass function, or PMF, gives the probability that a discrete random variable lands exactly on a given value. It also goes by discrete probability density function, probability function or frequency function. A PMF is often the main way to define a discrete probability distribution. It works for a single random variable or for several considered together.

paragraphs.heading: Mass, not density
paragraphs.text: A PMF differs from a probability density function, or PDF, which belongs to continuous random variables. With a PDF, you have to integrate over an interval to get a probability. For a discrete variable, P(X = x) = 1 means that event is certain, and P(X = x) = 0 means it can never happen. That reading fails for a continuous variable, where the chance of any one exact value is 0.

paragraphs.heading: Why call it mass
paragraphs.text: The mass picture helps prevent mistakes. Just as physical mass is conserved, so is the total probability spread over all possible outcomes. A PMF is zero everywhere except at a countable number of values of x. The value carrying the most probability mass is called the mode.

paragraphs.heading: Standard examples
paragraphs.text: Three major distributions go with PMFs: the Bernoulli, binomial and geometric distributions. The binomial counts successes over n draws made with replacement, each independent and with two possible outcomes. One case is the chance of getting exactly one 6 in three rolls of a fair die. The geometric counts the trials needed for one success, with PMF p_X(k) = (1 − p)ᵏ⁻¹p, as when you toss a coin until the first heads.

paragraphs.heading: Infinitely many outcomes
paragraphs.text: A PMF can cover endlessly many outcomes. Give every positive integer i the probability 1/2ⁱ. The masses still add up to 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ⋯ = 1. So the rule that total probability must be one still holds.

paragraphs.heading: Several variables
paragraphs.text: Two or more discrete random variables share a joint PMF, giving the probability of each combination of their values. The multinomial distribution is one example. Its random variables are the numbers of successes in each category after a set number of trials. The categorical distribution covers the case of a single trial in which one of two or more categories occurs.
